items.title: 企鹅殖民地评论：一款大胆怪异的恐怖游戏，其氛围和惊喜克服了其粗糙的边缘
items.summary: Something ancient and horrible stirs in the farthest south: Are you bad enough penguin to… not really do much

content.v: What is it? Lovecraftian horror through the eyes of a penguin. Release date October 16, 2026 Expect to pay $15 / £13 Developer Origame Digital Publisher Fellow Traveller Reviewed on RX 9070 XT, Core i5 12600K, 32 GB RAM, Steam Deck Multiplayer No Steam Deck Verified Link Steam

Penguin Colony is a work of cosmic horror that I would recommend to anyone with even a passing interest in scares from the beyond , even though its unique penguin platforming can be frustrating to wrangle. It's a radical recontextualization of an H.P. Lovecraft classic with a clear affection for the writer's storytelling, but also scathing contempt for his racism.

For my money, it's not October without a weird-ass new indie horror game leaving a lasting impression on me, and Penguin Colony has satisfied my annual craving. You are a penguin witnessing the events of the Lovecraft story, At the Mountains of Madness. Your powers are honk, slide, swim, and hop.

Rather than being limited to a specific bird, you are able to possess any penguin you come across, theoretically using different species' abilities to tackle different movement challenges. Aside from using little baby penguins to squeeze into tight spaces, I was almost exclusively a Rockhopper main: Their impressive vertical jump was a boon in many areas. They shoulda hooped instead of investigating The Strange.

The GOAT, PC Gamer Tales from The Hard Drive host Lenval Brown, narrates the adventure from the perspective of a customarily neurotic and verbose Lovecraft protagonist. Brown's delivery lends everything a similar emotional weight to his iconic performance in Disco Elysium, and he makes for a comforting, familiar presence⁠ even as things go all nasty crazy style.
Waddle on
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/Cxej37DiqTGbmNYWDKwS33-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/cUtDZakyX6iQXJaUF3Zfz-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/5ECkkFfbSHe3evfsEV8tu-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/cVQwBrkT4eNZ9XKsAgot23-1920-80.jpg

I remain conflicted over Penguin Colony's movement and mechanics: I didn't find them especially fun , they got in the way, but that also felt weirdly appropriate. As a penguin, waddling around is kinda shitty and sluggish, particularly as the levels shift away from their native habitat.

Most charitably, there's a Foddian (Getting Over It, Baby Steps ) quality to the mechanical exploration. It got me to really lean in for some tricky traversal as the atmosphere reached its most suffocating and intense in the caves and structures deep under the arctic ice⁠. I felt frustrated and restless as Penguin Colony's coolest levels opened up before me, held back as I was by this little penguin body. But that dovetails quite well with Penguin Colony's whole premise: that you are an inhuman observer of a human (and something else) story.

A more clear-cut negative was an inconsistency with a mantling ( do penguins mantle? ) feature ( was this intentional? ) that felt more like a clipping glitch, letting me clear some ledges but not others. Penguin Colony's appropriately minimalist UI has one glaring exception: A Shadow of the Colossus-style circular stamina meter that appears only when your stamina is depleting. It is distractingly massive and neon-colored, and it usually wasn't clear what the relationship was between what I was doing and the stamina bar's drain. It had a mind of its own, and was never a welcome sight during my playtime.

At its best, though, the penguin parkour contributed to this feeling that I was a small, insignificant thing skirting the edges of a drama I only partially understood. We as humankind are effectively unknowable elder gods to the rest of the animal kingdom, and Penguin Colony largely succeeded in evoking a one-of-a-kind sense of dual-layer cosmic horror through its mechanics.
Side stories

None of what follows is an explicit "Vader is Luke's da" spoiler, but this is definitely a game that thrives on surprise and interpretation. If you are already convinced you'd like to play, please leave the browser tab open⁠—ideally on multiple devices and refreshing regularly⁠—until you've completed Penguin Colony. Then come back and finish reading.

Penguin Colony is not a 1:1 retelling of At the Mountains of Madness. Lenval Brown voices a new character named Howard Blakely⁠—as opposed to the original story's William Dyer⁠—and the passages he narrates are a pitch-perfect imitation of Lovecraft's distinctive prose.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/mVsQw4pHeCc8hiNgbbk5nQ-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/L9tsX4WyxiAvsxAeoGSPZQ-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/wzDnjy42KTPqM4tgFBAimQ-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/P4Q6SAkPgEgufpXMSMWekQ-1920-80.jpg

Each level ends with a brief interlude where you control members of a party of Māori warriors who inherited a tradition of fighting and containing the evil at the south of the world. Blakely is a sympathetic American working with an expedition of Nazis, specifically their famous division devoted to finding The Ark of the Covenant, Thor's Hammer, the Easter Bunny, etc. The warriors are on a quest to stop the Nazis and suppress the outer evil they inadvertently awakened.

The war party interludes gradually built up the feeling that I was getting dispatches from another, "better" game. And I love that: I don't think I've ever played a game like Penguin Colony before, one where it feels like the full story is happening in another room, and I only get a keyhole view of what's really going on.

You get out what you put into this cryptic mystery: It's suffused with unique, cursive hieroglyphs, and I eventually realized that they're a replacement cipher for the alphabet. It pays to play with a notebook and pen nearby⁠—cracking this code was a rewarding little side activity that added to my understanding of the deeper plot.

The back half of Penguin Colony takes place among the twisting megastructures of an alien city under the ice, and Origame Digital manages to evoke an incredible sense of scale and ancient, terrible purpose with these levels: They reminded me of 2022's criminally underrated Scorn , as well as the stunning Ash Lake in Dark Souls' deepest depths. You don't fully understand what you're looking at, but you get that it is of a staggering profundity.
Case of the vapours

I notice a tendency in cosmic horror writing to shy away from the more unseemly aspects of H.P. Lovecraft's legacy, this instinct to say "Thank you for the outer horrors and cyclopean ruins, H.P., I'm going to tactfully gloss over what you named your cat, as well as your assorted thoughts on untermenschen, as though you are my least favorite uncle cornering me at a family gathering."

Penguin Colony proverbially says "fuck it, we ball" in this regard, making Lovecraft's racial fixations a very real, very impactful part of the horror. Blakely is an "enlightened" man of modernity who gets along just peachy with his expedition mates from the Third Reich. He is the neurotic, asylum-bound Lovecraft protagonist at his most cowardly, self-indulgent, and contemptible, and very much feels like a stand-in for old Howard Phillips himself.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/hFfQoPTJyiX98MidBvdtVf-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/S96wMsambZEw8uKtjU7acf-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/TnyhVcY5iNyPKhpw9jRHbf-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/3WZ6dmLucxkWvRrjwyqNcf-1920-80.jpg

The Māori warriors are everything Blakely is not, with minimal dialogue compared to Blakely's voluminous narration. Their laconic characterization is instead delivered through their actions and fellowship with each other. Their camaraderie stands in contrast with Blakely's solipsistic navel-gazing. They are proactive, and oppose the influence of outer beings rather than waiting to be changed by them. They are motivated to protect others, even to the point of self-sacrifice, in contrast with Blakely's vulgar, "scientific" curiosity or the Nazis' brutal nationalism.

items.title: 只要 RPG 存在，BioWare 令人难以置信的遗产就会继续下去
items.summary: EA is shutting down the venerable studio, but its impact will persevere.

content.v: https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ckZUwfxbakq5yXMJMfSmBW-1920-80.png

For my column this week I was going to write about climbing all over monsters in Dragon Dogma 2's chilly Dark Arisen expansion, but then EA decided to finally murder BioWare after years of slowly poisoning it. So sadly I am pivoting to this eulogy.

It's hard to discuss BioWare's demise without detailing the corporate meddling that led to one of gaming's most celebrated and enduring studios getting the axe. BioWare made mistakes, undeniably, but the buck stops at the executives who gutted its teams and never understood, for instance, the popularity of Dragon Age.
But things are bleak enough and you know all this already. So instead, I want to celebrate BioWare's impressive impact, which will continue for as long as studios are designing RPGs.

Even if BioWare ceased to exist after its incredible run of Infinity Engine games, it would still be considered an icon. Baldur's Gate was, for so many people, the CRPG, defining an era of roleplaying games and echoing across the decades. We're still talking about it, and studios are still designing games built on that old foundation.

Owlcat, Obsidian, Larian—three of the biggest RPG studios of the current era have all dipped into that well. Without BioWare we'd not have the Pathfinder CRPGs, Pillars of Eternity or Tyranny, and Baldur's Gate 3 certainly wouldn't exist.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/uKhJjjYSqE7VViixq9D9RX-1920-80.jpg

Obsidian as we know it would likely be a very different studio without BioWare, if it existed at all. It formed after the closure of Black Isle Studios, which published Baldur's Gate, and it relied on BioWare's Infinity Engine for Icewind Dale and Planescape: Torment. That relationship continued under Obsidian, with the team following up BioWare's Neverwinter Nights and KotOR with celebrated sequels, before making Pillars of Eternity , BG's spiritual successor.
Obsidian as we know it would likely be a very different studio without BioWare.

The modern resurgence of CRPGs, born out of a love of BioWare and Black Isle's library, probably would not have happened if the two studios had not made such a huge impression. Disco Elysium , for instance, owes a great deal to Planescape: Torment, and if ZA/UM had never created Disco, we wouldn't have games like Esoteric Ebb or Zero Parades either.

Following Baldur's Gate, BioWare gave us Neverwinter Nights in 2002, a game that was still undeniably a CRPG, but one that catered to the demand for 3D graphics. Neverwinter Nights was solid, but its real legacy was the Aurora Engine and the Aurora Toolset.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/xFqPoz4G2gGnFz3PYmTX3R-1920-80.jpg

BioWare gave players the power of game creation with the toolset, with which they spawned countless worlds, modules, mods and persistent servers—effectively community-run MMOs. It was my first foray into modding, when I created a D&D adventure for my flatmate's birthday. I was a broke student, so I couldn't afford a gift, but I could absolutely skive class and make a cool game.
Folks are still playing with the toolset today, in a community that has persevered for over two decades.

Also in 2002, a small Polish developer was founded. CD Projekt started life as a localisation studio, and it worked with BioWare and Interplay to create the Polish version of Baldur's Gate. From that relationship, it was given the job of porting Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance to PC. Unfortunately, that port was a victim of Interplay's demise, but bigger and better things were on the horizon.

The company formed a new studio to develop its own games, known as CD Projekt Red, and started work on the original Witcher. The studio then licensed the Aurora Engine from BioWare, which it heavily modified to create Geralt's first big videogame romp.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/R8C5wbhFsnmrFhRPtHiGvU-1920-80.jpg

CDPR's joint CEO Michał Nowakowski paid tribute to BioWare after the closure announcement, saying, "Bioware has been a massive part of CDPR history. We befriended them when localizing and selling Baldur’s Gate games in Poland, Czech, and Slovakia. And later they were [a] great help when lending us their engine for Witcher 1, sharing their wisdom and even giving us a spot at their booth at E3."
As the popularity of CRPGs started to wane and consoles began to dominate, BioWare adapted and pivoted.

As the popularity of CRPGs started to wane and consoles began to dominate, BioWare adapted and pivoted. Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic was still secretly a CRPG, but one that you could play on console with your controller, with so much of the classic CRPG complexity hidden from view.

KotOR kicked off a series that continued with KotOR 2, from Obsidian, and BioWare returned to the series for SWTOR, a MMO that continues today under developer Broadsword. At the time of its launch, it was the most expensive MMO ever made, and it continues to be an astonishing achievement in terms of the absurd amount of dialogue and voice acting.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/iUto3z5sS8sxsRQu8Zs69m-1920-80.jpg

With KotOR, BioWare really started to refine the features that would go on to influence so many RPGs (and games in other genres). BioWare RPGs have always featured big, game-changing decisions, letting you determine through your choices who lives, who dies, and who gets to become the protagonist's love interest. But in KotOR, we started to see this really become codified.

The romances, the alignment system, the ability to influence companions and even turn them to the Dark Side, these systems are part of the DNA of modern RPGs. Even now, we describe games that feature big, signposted story branches as having BioWare-style choices.

Jade Empire didn't make nearly as big a splash in 2005, but it's here we see BioWare experimenting with action-RPG mechanics. I love Jade Empire, and it further developed the BioWare-style choices, but it also felt a bit like it was following a trend rather than setting one. Story-driven action-RPGs weren't new.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/HhuDkt5xZvEjqXCNsiMyNi-1920-80.jpg

With Mass Effect, though, it attempted something different, and it was duly rewarded. KotOR and Jade Empire saw the studio try to adapt to changing tastes, but with Mass Effect BioWare had finally figured out how to move on from CRPGs.
BioWare had finally figured out how to move on from CRPGs.

The studio that gave us Baldur's Gate developing a third-person shooter sounded like a disaster waiting to happen, but instead BioWare made something incredible. Never before in a BioWare game had we been able to play such a well-defined protagonist, but the studio maintained the player agency it was so loved for, letting us create all these different versions of Shepard. There's so much more to the character than the binary Paragon/Renegade system.

Mass Effect is also where BioWare's experiments with choice and consequence really paid off. Do we wipe out an alien species or allow one of the galaxy's biggest threats to survive? Do we betray the Council or risk the deaths of countless humans? Do we date Liara or the space racist? And then we got to see these choices reverberate across the sequels. Years of decisions culminating in a fight for the galaxy's survival.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/QLBVemEasSnJmdfJ6VMfKF-1920-80.jpg

With BioWare's closure, we'll never get to see what it was planning for the fifth outing, though after Andromeda I'm not sure we would have been happy with it—even though the leaked trailer looks rad . But Mass Effect lives on. The Amazon series is reportedly still going forward , and not one but two new games are on the horizon that are carrying the torch: Owlcat's The Expanse: Osiris Reborn and Archetype's Exodus . Both are coming next year.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/bTQXAx999o9s5ZpdAgBv6B-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/L35AMDntFt4CuQc36M2mn-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/MB3P84zk7fGfWz3xXmAfMg-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/6offQUY4CXebir2TC27dMd-1920-80.jpg

items.title: 现在一切都结束了，《魔兽世界：永远》的测试版让我只剩下一种恐惧——它的结局
items.summary: How do you zig when all you know is zag?

content.v: https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PgGhmt5pTtxusaQQX3dHPF-1920-80.png

This is Terminally Online : PC Gamer's very own MMO column. Every other week, I'll be sharing my thoughts on the genre, interviewing fellow MMO-heads like me, taking a deep-dive into mechanics we've all taken for granted, and, occasionally, bringing in guest writers to talk about their MMO of choice.

World of Warcraft: Forever 's beta has just ended, and I'm basically sold, for now. I've had such a good time, in fact, that I dipped at around level 26 on my warrior (and 16 on a Shaman) because I didn't want to spoil or burn myself out before the full thing releases in November and I am consumed in a quest-drunk fugue.

But there is one thing that's rattling around in the back of my mind: This version of WoW is designed to be played perpetually (so in MMO terms, for about 10-20 years, give or take) at the level cap. There won't be any expansions, and the game will continue to expand horizontally.

Which leaves a major question hanging over its endgame. Now, collecting a few interviews together, we've seen a smidge of what that'll look like. In an interview with SkillUp , associate production director Clay Stone contrasts overtly horizontal progression systems (such as the Legacy tree) and gear, which he notes "our intention very much is to try to limit the amount of power progression as we release each raid tier."

Speaking to IGN Nordic , lead game designer Tim Jones says that "we're not going to make a Tier 2 raid without making the loot better … Tier 2 and Tier 3 raids will therefore have better gear, but we're going to be responsible about it. We still want gear from previous raids to remain useful, such as the Onslaught Girdle."
In other words, Forever'll still absolutely have a vertical progression, but your best-in-slot might include gear from all sorts of raids, which… oh, boy.

I'm not going to put a wooden plaque on my chest and say the end is nigh. If Forever's raid tiers only increase your overall item level by a couple of digits, then it really is not that much of a problem. It's essentially playing out that power creep in slow-motion, and if it takes a decade for there to be a numerical difference between, say, tier 1 and a hypothetical set of tier 10 gear that matters for more people than just hardcore min-maxers? It's all gravy, baby.

But as someone with a vested interest in these sorts of systems, I can't help but wonder if Blizzard is just making broad, sweeping assumptions about the way it has to do things at endgame. Forever is going to be purpose-built to keep folks in this rehashed version of classic Azeroth for a very long time. Is it not poison to the entire exercise, then, to purposefully introduce vertical progression at all?
Going up, up, up

I can see a few issues—or let's call them challenges —with this approach. Firstly, three tiers is manageable. But if Forever continues to add raid tiers, then those small incremental increases in gear power slowly stop becoming incremental at all.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/3yhvmXABMTiUYvTKkm3X27-1920-80.jpg

Unless a character can set foot in a tier 3 raid comfortably without getting gear from the first two tiers, what you've done is essentially created an attunement questline. That questline being, 'do several tiers of raiding to get up to snuff'.

In a game that resets every expansion, or season, this is a non-issue. But Forever'll have the task of bridging that gap the wider it gets—either with catch-up gear, which kills the older raids dead, or by issuing stat squishes, which never feels good on the other end of things.

The other problem is that, even if you do solve those problems, you've only got so many players. The wider the raiding scene is spread apart over the course of these raid tiers, the harder it becomes to find a group or a guild to do the specific raid that you need.

This can be solved, as these interviews mention, by giving each class useful best-in-slot gear from lower tiers so that they have an incentive to go back and do them. But there's another problem there, too: Characters only have so many equipment slots, and what's considered a BiS getup is dependent on a ton of other difficult-to-tune factors.

My point being: Blizzard really cannot rely on gearing to keep Forever's raiding scene alive in the long run, and yet (at least to start off with) it'll be mimicking old patterns. Just smaller, more controlled, and slower-paced. It's a little like trying to avoid an iceberg by designing the world's slowest boat. Sure, you're avoiding it for longer, but if you don't put a steering wheel on the damn thing you're gonna crash.
It's a little like trying to avoid an iceberg by designing the world's slowest boat.

This is by far Forever's biggest risk. Playing the game casually is going to rock. Questing is going to rock. Levelling alts is going to rock. Forever has already convinced me of all of these things—but the delicate, finickity balance of a pseudo-horizontal endgame is far harder.

You have to wonder if a developer who has been designing linear progression systems for over two decades is simply finding it hard to break from that ingrained patterning. Jones' words: "We're not going to make a tier 2 raid without making the loot better." They're sticking in my craw, because… well, why not ? Why are there tiered raids to begin with?

You could do as Guild Wars 2 does—new classes or skill trees to unlock that require endgame feats, character power for specific zones that'll stay relevant in perpetuity, an equivalent of "masteries". Basically, expanding the definition of what endgame is, and then having raids be a part of that ecosystem, rather than trying to slow-death power creep.

Blizzard's going to have to learn some very hard lessons to get there, though. I think this attitude towards tiers will work absolutely fine for a while, but there will come a point where the developer has to wonder if it wants to keep kicking the can down the road or really, genuinely reinvent what an endgame is in World of Warcraft. And that'll be either very exciting or very, very messy. Perhaps both.

items.title: New Blood 首席执行官证实：销售像 Gloomwood 和 Fallen Aces 这样的沉浸式模拟游戏最糟糕的方式就是称它们为沉浸式模拟游戏
items.summary: "It's not a good marketing term. And I don't think it helps."

content.v: Fans of Deus Ex, Dishonored and Gloomwood like to roll the words 'immersive sim' around their mouths as often as possible, savouring the fond associations with first-person drawer-rifling and guilt-ridden murder.

Yet there's something like consensus emerging among the makers of these games: it's really hard to sell an immersive sim while calling it by its name. "Is it a good marketing term? No," says New Blood Interactive CEO Dave Oshry. "It sucks. It's awful."
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PN49fLBoCxDm8tpDqKuXLR-1920-80.jpg

New Blood was first known for its boomer shooters, namely Dusk and Ultrakill , but has sunk years into two early access imsims, the well-regarded Gloomwood and Fallen Aces . Oshry likes to joke that he's "dumping all the money into immersive sims so we can go broke like the great studios that came before us, like Looking Glass."

Yet he'd never heard the term immersive sim until Gloomwood lead Dillon Rogers started work on his Thief-and-Resi-riffing open world. "He's like, 'That's what these are called'. I'm like, 'I have never heard that before in my life. What the fuck are you talking about?'"

Oshry wasn't new to the genre. He'd grown up adoring Deus Ex and Thief. "But Thief was a stealth game," he protests. "I called it a stealth game. Deus Ex I called an FPS-RPG because it was an FPS, but it was an RPG. You had points that you put in stuff. That's what an RPG is, like Diablo."
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/LWJqcFFvfrZySZj5CgRwGL-1920-80.jpg

Of course, ploughing points into skills and traits is something that's proliferated across mainstream games of all kinds in the decades since. But it's true: back in the year 2000, it was largely the preserve of RPGs. Deus Ex, with its dialogue, narrative choices and deadly greasel combat seemed a natural enough addition to that genre.

"System Shock and Deus Ex, they were RPGs," Oshry says. "People called them RPGs. That's the funny thing about an immersive sim. You're immersed in this world. You're building your character. Yeah, that's called an RPG, brother. That's a roleplaying game."

Does this age-old squabble over definitions really matter, so long as the games are good? Well, perhaps it does. Because immersive sims are considered to be niche and unworkable by many major publishers. Whereas RPGs? "They make lots of money and sell lots of copies," Oshry says. "You could argue that Baldur's Gate 3 is an immersive sim, because of the way that Larian builds their games. It's not first-person but you can stack boxes and use spells to pull things towards you and solve problems in unique ways."
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/QeCfENeW8J9Kg2QKLdpagQ-1920-80.jfif

The argument is one I've heard made before—in fact, I've even heard senior Larian developers refer to their Forgotten Realms opus as an immersive sim. But you won't find that phrase anywhere in its trailers or on its Steam page. "If you market something as an RPG, I think you'll do better than marketing it as an immersive sim," Oshry says.

A couple of years ago, Arkane founder Raphael Colantonio told me the same thing. "Nobody wonders what an RPG is," he said. "We might debate whether the Bethesda RPGs are an immersive sim or not, but who cares? The market just understands what an RPG is. Same with Baldur's Gate. If you say, 'This is an immersive sim,' you're going to have a tiny percentage of people that are super excited because they know what it means. And then the other ones, they're going to be like, 'What is it?'"

During the making of Arkane's Prey, the developer wasted lots of time explaining to its intended audience what an imsim was. Time that might have been better spent selling potential players on the joyous possibilities of the gloo cannon. Bethesda was disappointed by Prey's sales, and set the studio to work on Redfall instead—a route that ultimately led to Arkane Austin's closure under Xbox.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/UqfzUB8yrcHHZqajxp9jLf-1920-80.jpg

You could argue that 'immersive sim' is an inside baseball term that broke containment. For the alumni of Looking Glass, it was crucial—a way of codifying a shared set of principles in a '90s era when the vocabulary of game design was far from locked down. Figures like Warren Spector began to spread its use through interviews and postmortems . And for fans, adopting the term felt a little like joining a club.

"I think the term immersive simulation, if you know what that is, then you know what you're getting," Oshry says. "'Oh, cool! It's a game where I can solve problems by stacking boxes and crawling through vents and stabbing people in the back.' But it's not a good marketing term. And I don't think it helps. It's very niche, because if you say immersive sim, people are like, 'So it's a simulator?' Mainstream people have no idea what that means, and the people who know what it means, you didn't have to sell it to them anyway. Because they're looking for games like that."

When New Blood first started promoting Gloomwood, Oshry attempted to sidestep the imsim problem, but created a new one. "In my marketing genius, I was like, 'Let's call it Thief with guns,'" he says. "It's an easy sell. But it's a blessing and a curse bringing in all these fans of the Thief games who expect all these things from you. And Gloomwood's obviously not just Thief with guns, it takes from Call of Cthulhu and Resident Evil. Like most of our games, it's a mishmash of so many genres. 'Thief with guns' was a really easy elevator pitch. But it comes with a lot of expectations."
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/xK2k9HXz24SRMfC6MLR8U7-1920-80.jpg

By contrast, 'boomer shooter' has proven to be a straightforwardly useful marketing term throughout New Blood's existence. "There's people who are like, 'What do you mean, boomer shooter? Boomers didn't play these games.'" Oshry says. "That's not what it means. Also, yes, they do. My dad was a boomer, he played these games. I guess John Romero and John Carmack are Gen X, but Sandy Peterson sure as fuck is a boomer. But you say boomer shooter, people know exactly what it is. Yeah, it's a game like Doom and Quake and stuff."

You'll notice that, when New Blood bundles Gloomwood and Fallen Aces together with the Stalker-like Blood West on Steam, they're collectively called 'the stealth trilogy'. "Because that's what draws people in," Oshry says. "If we called it the immersive sim trilogy, nobody would fucking buy the games."
